body: Psycholinguistics is a disciplinary framework for mapping the mental representations and processes underlying language production, comprehension, and acquisition. Parameters: processing models, lexical access, syntactic parsing, memory constraints, experimental paradigms, developmental stages. It persists via peer-reviewed experiments, cognitive models, laboratory protocols, and university curricula that replicate findings across populations.

Sociolinguistics is a disciplinary framework for mapping systematic correlations between linguistic variation and social structure. Parameters: speech community, social variables (class, gender, age, ethnicity, region), linguistic variables (phonetic, lexical, syntactic, pragmatic), interactional context and language ideology. It persists via peer-reviewed publications, university curricula, research corpora, and methodological protocols that replicate observations across speech communities.

Computational linguistics is a disciplinary framework for formalizing linguistic knowledge in algorithms and computational models. Parameters: corpus design, statistical models, symbolic grammars, evaluation metrics, processing pipelines. It persists via open-source software, benchmark datasets, peer-reviewed publications, and university curricula that replicate model performance across tasks.

Linguistic register is the map of the system of situationally differentiated language varieties a speech community develops and maintains — the varieties a community deploys for different communicative situations (colloquial, formal, technical, ceremonial, professional) — carved along three parameters. (1) The situational axis: the dimensions along which the varieties are organized are field (the subject matter and activity in which the language is deployed), tenor (the social relations and roles between participants), and mode (the channel and the participatory structure of the discourse); a variety is a conventionalized set of lexical, grammatical, and prosodic choices indexed to the situation, so that the same speaker deploys different varieties in different situations. (2) The boundary lines that separate the map from its neighbours: register is indexed to situation, which distinguishes it from dialect (indexed to region and social group) and from genre (a type of discourse text rather than a variety of the language itself); and it is distinct from the institutional register — an official list maintained by an authority with legal or institutional force — in that a linguistic register is updated by the speech community's convention, not by institutional mandate, and no authority stands behind its entries. (3) The map, not the territory: the entry names the systematic description the community and the discipline build over the natural variation of speech — the inventory of varieties and the dimensions that organize it — not the natural variation itself. Persistence: the varieties persist as social convention — acquired in socialization, maintained through institutional reinforcement (courts, academies, professions, liturgy), and relearned by each generation; the map persists as the stable sub-field of linguistics called register analysis, its dimensions codified in textbooks and corpora. Historical linguistics is a disciplinary framework for reconstructing diachronic change in language systems from attested corpora. Parameters: comparative method, sound change laws, attestation dates, textual corpora, reconstruction techniques. It persists via published reconstructions, philological editions, comparative datasets, and university curricula that transmit methodological standards across generations.
